prompt: Write a first-person detective story featuring a locked-room murder case. The story should be tightly plotted with strong suspense.

outline.name: The Telegram
outline.description: Victor Hale, a disgraced former homicide detective now scraping by on insurance fraud cases, receives an urgent telegram from Arthur Pemberton: 'He is alive. Come to Blackwood Peak. If I am found dead, the answer is in the wall.' Victor had once dismissed Arthur's paranoid letters as ramblings, but the enclosed bank draft is enough to make him accept. He takes the funicular up to the isolated Blackwood Peak Hotel, a converted Victorian mansion stranded on a glacier, just as a blizzard buries the tracks behind him. At dinner he meets the other stranded guests: Marcus Webb, Arthur's resentful business partner; Celia Pemberton, Arthur's estranged actress wife; Ruth Keene, his devoted secretary; and Elias, a strange night porter. Arthur never appears. That night, Victor is woken by a scream from the east wing.

outline.name: The Locked Door
outline.description: Victor breaks into Arthur's suite with Sheriff Calder, his old rival from the city force. The heavy oak door is bolted from the inside with a solid brass bolt. The windows are frosted shut, sealed by a century of paint. The chimney is too narrow for even a child. Arthur Pemberton lies dead near the fireplace, two deep stab wounds in his chest and a defensive gash across his forearm. Calder declares it suicide, mocking Victor's ruined career. Victor points out that no man stabs himself twice and then slashes his own arm in self-defense. He takes charge of the scene, searching for a weapon that is nowhere to be found. The room is sealed, the body is murdered, and the killer has vanished into thin air.

outline.name: The Suspects
outline.description: Victor and Calder interview the trapped guests. Marcus Webb claims he was drinking alone in the lounge, but no one can confirm it. Celia says she was in her room with a headache, yet her story is shaky and her hands are cold. Ruth Keene was supposedly typing, but she is evasive and keeps clutching her purse. Elias, the porter, swears that just before the scream he saw a dark shadow pass under Arthur's door—and then heard Arthur cry out, 'You're dead!' Each suspect has a motive: Marcus faced financial ruin, Celia was about to be cut off, Ruth's position depended on Arthur's will, and Elias seems to know more than he admits. Calder insists the locked room makes suicide the only possible answer, but Victor refuses to accept it. The blizzard has cut them off from the world; the killer is still among them.

outline.name: The Letter
outline.description: Victor returns to the suite alone, hoping to find something the others missed. In the inner pocket of Arthur's coat, he finds a letter addressed to him, written hours before the murder. Arthur repeats his warning: his twin brother, Silas, presumed dead in a boating accident twenty years ago, is alive and hiding in the hotel. 'He knows the old ways of this house. If I am found dead, the answer is in the wall.' Victor is flooded with guilt—he had dismissed the earlier letters as paranoid rambling. He re-tests the locked room: bolt, windows, chimney. No exit. Yet the letter insists. He begins tapping the walls and discovers a seam in the wainscoting. He pries it open and finds a narrow dark opening.

outline.name: The Priest-Hole
outline.description: Victor opens the hidden panel and finds a priest-hole: a narrow vertical compartment just wide enough for a man. The dust has been recently disturbed. There are fresh footprints, a dropped cufflink, and a faint smell of tobacco. But the back wall appears to be solid brick, and Victor concludes the killer could not have hidden there—there is no exit. He pockets the cufflink and dismisses the space as a dead end. Ruth Keene interrupts him, claiming she was looking for Arthur's will. She grows uneasy when she sees the open panel. After she leaves, Victor stares at the priest-hole and realizes the line of the brick is too regular to be natural. Before he can investigate further, another scream echoes through the corridor.

outline.name: The Shadow Under the Door
outline.description: The second scream turns out to be Celia, startled by a rat—or so she says. Victor is not convinced. He returns to Elias and forces him to repeat his account. Before the murder, a shadow slid across the band of light beneath Arthur's door, and then Arthur cried out. Victor reconstructs the scene: the door was bolted from inside, the room was lit, and the shadow came from someone moving inside the room. If Arthur had been alone, he could have made the shadow himself—but Elias heard Arthur scream at someone. That means a second person was inside the sealed room when the bolt was thrown. Victor realizes the killer must have been hiding in the room before Arthur locked himself in. The only hiding place is the priest-hole. He rushes back to the suite, determined to find the secret he missed.

outline.name: The Forged Signature
outline.description: Before Victor can reach the priest-hole, he catches Ruth Keene in Arthur's study, burning a document. He rescues it from the fire: a power-of-attorney transferring all of Arthur's assets to Ruth. The signature is a clumsy tracing from an old contract. Ruth breaks down and confesses she forged it, but swears she was trying to protect Arthur from Marcus Webb, who had been stealing from the company. She admits she saw Marcus enter Arthur's room earlier that night. Marcus denies it, and Celia retaliates by revealing that Ruth and Marcus were once lovers. The motives are multiplying, but the locked room still makes no sense. As Ruth leaves, Victor notices a smear of grease on her sleeve—the same grease from the priest-hole floor. He realizes she has been inside the hidden compartment too. He rushes back to the suite.

outline.name: The Boiler Room
outline.description: Victor returns to the priest-hole and, with a penknife, finds the spring catch in the false brick panel. The back of the compartment swings open, revealing a narrow service passage that winds down through the walls of the hotel. Victor follows it to an iron door that opens into the boiler room. There, hidden in an alcove, he finds a wet coat, a knife wrapped in oilcloth, and a faded photograph of two identical boys. Footsteps echo behind him. Silas Pemberton steps out of the shadows—gaunt, bearded, very much alive. He tells Victor he has been living in the forgotten passages of the hotel for days. Before Victor can draw his gun, Silas strikes him down. Victor collapses onto the concrete floor, the truth burning in his mind.

outline.name: The Twin
outline.description: Victor wakes tied to a pipe in the boiler room. Silas is feeding the murder weapon into the furnace. He speaks calmly, revealing everything: twenty years ago, he survived the boating accident, but Arthur left him to drown in order to claim the family inheritance. Silas has been hiding ever since, waiting for his chance. He entered Arthur's suite through the priest-hole before Arthur threw the bolt, killed him, and escaped through the hidden passage—creating a perfect locked room. The shadow Elias saw under the door was Silas crossing the room before the murder. Victor keeps Silas talking, appealing to the brother Arthur feared, until Sheriff Calder, following Victor's earlier note, bursts in with Elias. They overpower Silas and drag him into the light. Calder admits he was wrong. The locked room was never sealed—the killer had already been inside.

outline.name: Redemption
outline.description: The blizzard breaks, and the funicular is repaired. Silas is taken away, and the hidden passage is exposed to the authorities. Victor stands in the cold morning light, looking at the room that almost defeated him. He realizes the locked room was not a puzzle of bolts and walls, but a prison of his own perception. He had insisted the room was sealed because he could not accept that his judgment might be wrong—the same arrogance that had destroyed his career and cost an innocent man his freedom. He writes a letter of apology to Arthur's memory, and a second letter to the court, reopening the old wrongful conviction. The key to the locked room was never a key at all. It was a man who had already been inside—and the door Victor had to open was the one to his own closed mind.

chapters.name: The Telegram
chapters.content:
The office smelled of stale coffee and older regrets. I sat at a desk the size of a coffin, sorting through other people's disasters for Goliath Insurance—hunting fraud in the fine print. It paid the rent. It did not pay the shame. Once I'd been a homicide detective with a clearance rate that made my superiors nervous. Then the Armitage case broke me: I was so certain of the guilty man that I doctored nothing, just ignored everything that didn't fit. An innocent man went to prison, the real killer walked free, and the badge went the way of my reputation.

The telegram came at four. Thin paper, the crest of Blackwood Peak Hotel.

HE IS ALIVE. COME TO BLACKWOOD PEAK. IF I AM FOUND DEAD, THE ANSWER IS IN THE WALL.

No signature. Arthur Pemberton was the only man I knew who spoke entirely in capital letters and doom. For two years his letters had arrived with the regularity of bad weather—rambling, then frantic, then outright paranoid. Someone watching him from the funicular. Someone in the walls. His food tasted of metal. The last letter had ended: they mean to bury me alive. I had answered twice, suggesting a physician. Then I'd stopped answering. I called it paranoia. The word tasted like ash.

The second sheet was a bank draft for enough to clear my debts three times over. Arthur wasn't asking me to come. He was buying me.

And he was saying his brother was alive. Twenty years ago, Silas—Arthur's twin—had drowned in a boating accident on the glacier lake. No body. Arthur inherited everything and spent two decades seeing his brother's face in every shadow. I'd called it madness. Now the madman was paying me to believe him.

The funicular climbed the mountain like a dying prayer. I was the only passenger; the car was ancient, painted peeling red, groaning against its cable as the valley fell away and the pines thinned to black scratches. Snow began an hour into the ascent—the hard, driving sort that erased the world beyond the windows. By the time the car shuddered to a stop, the tracks behind us had vanished. We were not arriving. We were being swallowed.

Blackwood Peak Hotel stood against the grey sky like something that had grown there: a Victorian mansion gone to seed, gables and blind-eyed windows, a glacier pressing against its eastern wall like a tongue slowly eating the stone. The man who took my bag moved like a coffin bearer. Elias, he said, in a voice like gravel. Pale, narrow face; eyes that watched the corridor behind me rather than my own. "You're the last one. The morning car won't run."

"Then I'm stranded."

"You're a guest," he said, as though the two were different.

The hotel was warm inside, overlit in a way that left shadows in the corners anyway. A fire crackled in the lounge, and around it the other guests were arranged like pieces on a board. Above the fireplace hung a portrait of two boys in identical sailor suits, faces so alike they might have shared one mirror. The smile on the left boy looked like a dare. I looked away and found Elias watching me watch it.

Celia Pemberton, Arthur's wife, wore her beauty like a coat she'd forgotten to take off. She drank wine and stared at the flames with the practiced vacancy of an actress aware she was being watched. Marcus Webb, Arthur's business partner, was broad and red-faced, a glass of whiskey in his fist, the look of a man who had been drinking for hours and intended to continue. At a writing desk, a thin dark-haired woman typed without looking up—Ruth Keene, Arthur's secretary. I knew her name from the letters.

Elias served dinner. Arthur did not appear. The chair at the head of the table stayed empty, and Webb kept glancing at it as if expecting it to speak.

"He'll be down when he's ready," Celia said, answering the question no one had asked. "He's always in his room these days. Working." She said the word like it was a disease.

Webb grunted. "Or hiding. He's been talking about ghosts again." He looked at me, glassy-eyed but sharp. "You're the detective he hired. Heard about you."

"Then you know why he hired me."

"Because he's afraid of his own shadow," Webb said. "And now he's paid yours to stand in it."

I turned to Ruth. "When did you last see him?"

Her fingers paused over the keys. "This morning. He dictated his correspondence and asked me to seal the envelopes." She said it carefully, like a witness choosing her words. "He seemed... tired. Not afraid. Tired."

Celia laughed—a short, glittering sound. "He's been tired for twenty years. It's his only subject."

Ruth resumed typing. At the end of the room, Elias stood in the doorway with his tray, motionless, as if he had always been there.

The dinner ended without Arthur. I went to my room and lay awake, the wind screaming against the glass, listening to the old house settle and creak around me. The telegram was folded in my coat pocket. The answer is in the wall. What kind of answer? And what kind of wall? At midnight I thought I heard footsteps in the corridor outside my door—slow, deliberate. Then nothing. I told myself it was Elias on his rounds. I eventually drifted off.

The scream ripped me out of sleep like a hook. It came from the east wing, high and thin, cut short. I was on my feet before my eyes were open, heart pounding, and I knew that voice. Arthur's voice—I knew it the way you know the sound that will change everything.

Then I was running.

chapters.name: The Locked Door
chapters.content:
The scream ended the way a throat ends under water—abrupt, swallowed. I ran.

The east wing was a corridor of shut doors. I found Arthur's suite by the brass plate on the wall and put my shoulder into the oak. It didn't give. The wood was old, the frame settled around it like a fist.

Boots came down the hall. "Hale." Sheriff Calder, muffled in a sheepskin coat, a key ring in hand. We had known each other once, before the force showed me the door and this county gave him a star. "That's Arthur's room. I've been told to keep an eye on him."

"He screamed."

"We all heard." He tried the key. The latch turned. The door didn't move. He pushed, grunted, pushed again.

"It's bolted," I said. I dropped to a knee and squinted at the gap between door and frame. A bright edge of brass showed in the crack, thick as a thumb and thrown hard into its keeper. On the inside.

We hit the door together. The frame groaned. Twice more, and the oak splintered around the lock. The fourth charge tore the screws clear of the wood, and the door swung inward, spilling a heavy brass bolt across the floor like a coin.

The room smelled of coal dust and blood.

Arthur Pemberton lay on the rug before the hearth. His dressing gown was dark with two wounds high in the chest, each the width of a blade. His fingers were curled as if he'd tried to hold the blood in. There was a long gash along his forearm, the edges clean and white where skin had parted. His eyes were open. The fire had burned to embers.

Calder looked down at him. "Well. There it is."

"Someone killed him."

"Someone." He gestured at the door. "That was bolted, you said. Look at the room." He turned a slow circle. "One door. We broke it open." He looked at the windows.

I went to them. Two tall sashes, the glass frosted with ice, the frames painted shut by what looked like a century of layered paint. I pressed on the sills, tried the lower halves. Neither moved. The dust along the meeting rail was unbroken—no one had pushed these up in years.

"The chimney?"

I knelt at the hearth. The opening was wide, but the flue pinched in quickly, narrowing to a channel half the width of my shoulders, too narrow for a child. I reached in and brought out soot, undisturbed, a clean skin of it. Nothing had come down. Nothing had gone up.

"Windows sealed," I said. "Chimney impossible. Door bolted from inside."

"Which means he did it himself." Calder squatted by the body. "Rich man, sick in the head. Everyone here knows he'd been writing mad letters."

"He didn't do this himself."

"Because?"

I pointed. "Two wounds in the chest. A man who wants to die takes one deep stab, maybe two. But look at his arm." I lifted Arthur's wrist, gently. The gash ran along the outside of the forearm, a long defensive cut. "That's a wound you get when you throw your arm up to block a blade. He didn't stab himself twice and then cut his own arm defending himself from his own hand."

Calder's jaw worked. "It could've happened any way."

"Then where's the weapon?" I searched the room—the hearth, the grate, the ashes, the sideboard, the desk drawers, the bureau, the wingback chairs, behind the curtains, under the bed in the adjoining room. Nothing. No blade. No knife. No letter opener.

"If he killed himself," I said, "the knife would have fallen beside him. It would be here. It's not. Someone removed it."

"Removed it how? The door was bolted from the inside. You saw it."

I had no answer.

Calder straightened. "You want to tell me the killer walked through the wall?"

"Maybe."

"Jesus, Hale." His voice dropped into something almost like pity, which was worse than mockery. "This is what I'm telling you. You build the case first, then bend the facts to fit it. That's what happened with Armitage. You were so sure—so certain you had the whole thing in your head—and the man you put in prison took eight years of his life before the rest of us found out he was innocent." He held out his hand, palm up, offering me the lesson. "The facts are the facts. This was a locked room, and the only man in it is dead by his own hand."

"You don't believe that."

"I believe in going home at the end of my shift."

I looked down at Arthur Pemberton. His face wore the slack look of a man who had been afraid for a long time and then, abruptly, had stopped being afraid at all. He had written me letters for two years. I had read the first few, decided they were a rich man's fancies, and let the rest thicken in a drawer. The telegram came three days ago: *He is alive. Come to Blackwood Peak. If I am found dead, the answer is in the wall.*

I hadn't believed him. I had come for the bank draft that would clear my debts and told myself it was an old man's paranoia.

But the facts were the facts. I had learned that lesson once, in the worst possible way. The facts here were impossible: the door bolted, the windows sealed, the chimney too narrow, two stab wounds over a defensive one, no weapon in the room. I was not going to make the same mistake twice by deciding what the truth was before I'd seen all of it.

"Leave the room as it is," I said.

"You don't make calls here."

"I'm asking. Seal it. Let the blizzard blow out. In the morning I'll look again."

Calder met my eyes. "You'll find the same body and the same room."

"Maybe."

"Maybe isn't a case."

I looked at Arthur's hand, the fingers curled around nothing. "It's a start."

chapters.name: The Suspects
chapters.content:
The lounge had gone cold. The fire had burned down to a heap of ash while we were breaking down Arthur's door, and nobody had thought to feed it since. The five of us stood in a loose circle—Calder with his sheepskin collar turned up, the guests wrapped in whatever they had grabbed, the portrait of the two boys watching over our shoulders from above the mantel. From the windows, the blizzard pressed its white face against the glass and howled.

Calder started with the business partner. Marcus Webb had posted himself by the sideboard with a glass of something amber, and he was well into his third. His red face had gone blotchy.

"I was here," he said. "Right here in this lounge. From after dinner until the scream. Drinking alone, because nobody else wanted to keep me company. You can ask the room."

"The room can't confirm it," I said.

"Then I'm a murderer because I prefer my own company?" He set the glass down too hard. "Arthur and I had our differences. Every partner has differences. But I didn't climb through a locked door to stick a knife in him."

Calder asked about their business. Webb's jaw tightened.

"Arthur thought I was stealing from him. That's a lie." He said it too quickly. "He'd been threatening to bring in auditors. If he'd lived, he might have found nothing at all, and apologized, and we would have gone on."

"Or," I said, "he might have found everything."

Webb's hand trembled. He picked up his glass, put it down. "I was in this room."

Celia Pemberton was next. She had not changed out of the dinner dress she'd worn hours earlier, and the wine in her glass was nearly untouched. She sat on the edge of a velvet chair as if it were a stage prop.

"I had a headache," she said. "I took two powders and lay in the dark. I heard nothing at all until the screaming."

"Your husband was killed twenty yards from your door," I said.

"And I slept through the murder and woke for the scream. I'm a shallow sleeper, Mr.—" She paused, waiting for a name I did not give her. "I woke for the scream. There. Is that consistent enough?"

Her story was thin as paper. She could not say what time she'd gone to bed, what she'd taken, whether she'd undressed. She was still wearing her dress. I asked if she always slept in evening wear. She smiled with her mouth only.

"I didn't sleep at all," she said. "You want to know if I killed Arthur, and the answer is that I've wished him dead for years. But I never had the nerve." She touched my wrist, and her hand was cold as lake water. "If I'd had it, I wouldn't have done it that way. All that blood."

I took her coldness as spite, or fear, or both.

Ruth Keene sat apart from the others, a thin woman in a high-collared blouse, hands folded over a worn leather purse as if it were a lapdog. She told us she had been in the office annex, typing the letters Arthur had dictated that morning.

"I sealed them," she said.

"All evening?"

"I restarted the ones the old typewriter mangled." She did not look away, but her fingers tightened on the purse. "I didn't hear anything. The wind is loud in that corner of the house."

She was evasive in the way of someone used to being questioned. I asked what was in the purse. She said, with a flicker of displeasure, "Letters. Receipts. A woman's things." She did not open it.

I let it go. For now.

Elias was last. The servant had been standing by the door the whole time, quiet as a shadow, and when Calder waved him forward he came with his hands clasped behind his back.

"I was on the east wing corridor," he said. "The windows rattle in this weather. I was checking them so the guests could sleep."

"At midnight?" I asked.

"I am the night porter, sir."

"And you saw something?"

He took a breath. "There was a light beneath Mr. Pemberton's door. The band of it, across the floor. I was at the end of the corridor and I saw a shadow pass over it."

Calder grunted. "From outside?"

"There is no outside," Elias said. "The shadow was in the room. It moved toward the door, and it stopped under the light, as if whoever made it was standing there. Then Mr. Pemberton spoke. Through the door. He said—" The servant's throat worked. "He said, 'You're dead.'"

The words sat in the room like something solid. I thought about Arthur's letters. *They mean to bury me alive. He is in the walls.*

Calder shook his head. "That's a dying man's cry. He was raving."

"His voice was not afraid," Elias said quietly. "It was astonished. As if he had seen something that should not exist."

"Or someone," I said.

Calder turned on me. "Don't start building your house on a shadow and a dead man's words. You know what happens when you decide before you've got the facts."

The Armitage case hung between us. I felt it. Eight years of an innocent man's life, bought by my certainty. I had been so sure. The facts had fit. Except the one fact I'd ignored.

"I know exactly what happens," I said. "That's why I'm not deciding it's suicide because the door was bolted." I moved to the fireplace and turned to face them all. "Let's have motives, since we're all here."

Webb faced ruin—Arthur's auditors would have found his theft. Celia was about to be cut off; she'd told me herself that Arthur had threatened it every month, and a man who makes threats eventually signs the papers. Ruth's future depended on Arthur's will, and she had been looking for it when I found her near the suite—or so she claimed. And Elias, who knew the hotel's old ways better than anyone, was the one who told us about the shadow, which was either the truth or a lie told to point fingers elsewhere.

"When the snow clears," I said, "one of us will be able to explain all of this. But not yet."

Celia laughed, high and thin. "You think the killer will confess by morning?"

"The killer doesn't have to confess." I looked at each of them. "The room was sealed. Whoever did this is still here. Snow keeps us together. Time does the rest."

Calder told everyone to go to their rooms and stay there. They drifted away one by one—Webb muttering, Celia holding her wine, Ruth with her purse pressed to her chest, Elias last, watching the corridors behind people the way he always did.

I stood at the window with the blizzard's howl on the other side of the glass. Somewhere in this hotel, behind the walls, in the dark between the rooms, there was an answer. Arthur had sealed it himself. *If I am found dead, the answer is in the wall.*

I hadn't found the wall yet.

But I had time. The snow would hold us here until the truth came out—mine, and Arthur's, and the shape of whoever had watched him die through a locked door and then walked away leaving only a shadow and a dead man's last words.

chapters.name: The Letter
chapters.content:
The corridor was empty when I left my room. I had waited until the house went quiet—until Webb's muttering faded, until Celia's heels stopped their restless crossing, until even the wind paused. Then I took the passkey Calder had given me, lit a candle, and went to the east wing alone.

Arthur's door hung open where we had broken it, a chair wedged against the jamb. The brass bolt lay where it had fallen. I stepped over it. The oil lamp on the desk had drowned; the room smelled of tallow, cold ash, and the faint sweetness blood leaves when it has begun to cool.

Arthur lay where we had left him. Calder had covered his face with a handkerchief, but the dressing gown was still dark at the chest and the fingers were still curled. I knelt beside him, looking for what the first search had missed—and, I admit, wanting to be alone with him, the way you want to be alone with a man you have wronged after it is too late.

The first search had been thorough, but it had been a search for a weapon—under the cushions, in the embers, behind the bureau, beneath the bed. We had not looked for a message. Arthur had sent me one every other Tuesday for two years; I had read each one long enough to call it madness, and then burned it.

I found the envelope in the inner pocket of his dressing gown, folded against his heart. Unsealed, as if he had meant to hand it to me himself. It was addressed in his hand: *For Victor Hale. To be opened if I am not returned.*

The letter inside was dated that same evening.

*Hale,*

*You will not believe this. You have not believed anything I have written for two years, and I do not blame you. But I have seen him. Twice. Once aboard the funicular in the fog, on the rear platform where no passenger had boarded. Once tonight, at my window, on the outside of the glass.*

*Silas is alive. He is here, in this house, in the walls the way we hid in them as children. He knows the old ways of this house. He has been waiting twenty years.*

*You will say there was no body, that no man climbs out of a glacier lake after twenty years. You are wrong. He is the reason I wrote to you. He is the reason I tasted metal in my food and heard footsteps in the plaster.*

*I let him drown, Hale. I wanted the money, and I let the water take him. Now he has come back for what I owe him. I do not ask you to forgive me, but you are the only one who ever came when I called.*

*If I am found dead, the answer is in the wall.*

No signature. Below the last line he had drawn a little diagram: a square with a line through it, like a door without a frame.

I sat back on my heels, the paper trembling in my fingers. The cold in the room had got inside me now.

He had written to me for two years. Footsteps in the walls. Faces at the glass. *They mean to bury me alive.* I had read those letters in my rented room and told myself the man was lonely, the man was ill, the man had lived too long on his mountain. I had answered exactly one of them—a form letter, the kind I wrote for Goliath Insurance denying a claim. And he had kept writing anyway, because I was the only one who ever came when he called. I had come at last, a day too late, expecting to find a delusion.

The worst of it was that I had done this before. The Armitage case had not taught me to doubt my certainties; it had taught me to doubt the wrong things. I had dismissed the people in his walls because walls do not move. Now Arthur was dead in front of me, stabbed twice, his arm slashed in a fight he had lost, and whoever had done it had walked out of a sealed room.

No. Not walked. He had been inside when the bolt was thrown.

I got to my feet and went through the room again. The door: bolt shot from inside, strike plate scored with years of use. The windows: two tall arches glazed with frost, their painted rails unbroken, the dust on the sills thick enough to take a print—and no print but my own. The chimney: a throat too narrow for a child, soot undisturbed from hearth to sky.

Bolt. Windows. Chimney. I had tested them all before. I tested them again, because the letter insisted, and the walls went on being walls.

*The answer is in the wall.*

I pressed my palm flat against the wainscoting beside the hearth. The wood was cold and dark with a century of oil and hands. I knocked. Solid. I moved to the next panel and knocked again. I went around the room that way, tap, shift, tap, shift, like a man catching himself believing in ghosts. Wallpaper over plaster: dead. Panels under the bookshelves: dead. I had almost given up when I reached the wainscoting behind the writing desk, and my knuckles answered with a hollowness that was not quite empty.

I moved the desk, its legs scraping the floor. The house was still. I set the candle on the floor and studied the panel.

The grain was ordinary. The varnish was old. But the seam on the right side was too straight—the kind of line a tool cuts and a century of dirt disguises. I pressed my fingertips into it. Nothing. I worked my penknife in along the seam and felt the blade catch on iron, a latch worn thin by use.

I pressed it. The panel clicked and swung inward on hidden hinges, and the wall opened.

Cold air poured out, carrying dust and the smell of old brick. I held up the candle. The opening was narrow, barely a man's width, vanishing into blackness. At its threshold, in the dust of the floor, was a footprint that was not mine.

chapters.name: The Priest-Hole
chapters.content:
I took the lamp from the writing desk and stepped into the wall.

The passage was a priest-hole, one of those narrow vertical compartments built into old houses to hide a man from the men sent to kill him. This one was just wide enough to stand in with your arms at your sides, no more. It went up into darkness above and down below the level of the floor, and the air came out of it cold, tasting of old brick and dust and something older—the particular stillness of a place that has been waited in. Arthur had written that he and Silas hid in the walls as children. I had not believed him. The cold air said the letter was true.

The dust at my feet had been disturbed recently, in long dragging sweeps, and in the settled powder I found the print of a boot. Not a clear match, but the same tread that had left the print at the threshold, the one that was not mine. Someone had stood here, and stood long enough to leave his shape in the room.

Something glittered at the base of the wall. I bent and picked it up: a cufflink, plain and small, worked in some dull metal that was neither silver nor gold. It was warm against my cold fingers, as if it had been on a man's wrist within the hour. No monogram. I turned it over and saw nothing but the scratch of wear. I pocketed it.

Tobacco hung in the air. Faint, stale, the ghost of a smell rather than the smell itself. I had not seen a pipe, a pouch, or a tin in Arthur's suite. The odor did not belong to the room. It belonged to this dark hole and the man who had waited in it.

I held the lamp to the back wall and looked for a way out. Brick, old and soot-dark, laid in courses, the mortar black with age. I tapped along its length with the butt of my penknife and got no hollow answer. I went down on my knees and ran my hand along the base, pressed the bricks one by one, searched the floor for a seam. Nothing. The compartment was a dead end, sealed on all sides, a pocket in the heart of the wall with one way in and one way out, and that way was the panel I had come through.

I stepped out of the hole and stood still in the dead man's room, breathing. The killer could not have hidden here. There was no exit. And yet the door had been bolted from inside, the windows painted shut, the chimney too thin for a child. The arithmetic would not come out. That was the moment I nearly made the old mistake: forcing a solution onto facts that would not hold it. The Armitage lesson burned in me—build the case first, bend the facts, and an innocent man serves eight years. So I forced myself to admit the truth. The priest-hole was a dead end. Arthur's letter had led me to a wall, and the wall had led me to a box, and the box was empty. I had been wrong to believe him. Just as I had been wrong, for two years, not to.

"Mr. Hale."

The voice came from the doorway, soft and deliberate. Ruth Keene stood at the jamb, dark coat buttoned to her chin, her worn leather purse clutched in both hands. She had come through the broken door without a sound.

"I was looking for Mr. Pemberton's will," she said. The words were too even, a line she had practiced and delivered.

"The will is in the study, Miss Keene. Not in a dead man's room at midnight."

She did not answer. Her eyes had found the opening in the wall behind me, the dark mouth of the panel. The lamp was still in my hand, and her face moved in its light. The blood left it. She took a step back without meaning to.

"What is that?" she said.

"A priest-hole. You've worked for him how long, and you've never seen it?"

"No." Her eyes did not agree. They kept returning to the opening, and her hands had gone white around the purse. There was something in that purse she was protecting, or hiding from the sight of the hole. "I should not have come. I only wanted—" She stopped, and I saw her choose a safer word. "I wanted to be sure."

"Sure of what?"

She backed into the corridor, shaking her head. "I should not have come," she said again, to herself this time. Then she was gone, her footsteps rapid and fading into the dark of the east wing.

I turned back to the priest-hole and stared into it the way I had stared at a hundred rooms before I learned to see. And then I saw.

The line of the brick was too regular. A century of weight makes mortar wander; walls settle and breathe, and their courses take on a slow organic unevenness, the signature of time. This wall was too straight. The joints ran like ruled lines, the courses level from floor to top, the pattern too deliberate to be structural. It was not a wall that had been built around a space. It was a wall built to make a space look sealed.

Arthur's diagram. A square with a line through it. Like a door without a frame.

I reached for my penknife, and the scream hit the corridor.

It came from the east wing, a woman's voice, raw and full, cut off sharp as a broken string. The lamp shook in my grip; the flame jumped and steadied. I was already moving, past the bolted brass that had never been the answer, past the broken door, into the dark hall where the scream still hung in the air like frost.

chapters.name: The Shadow Under the Door
chapters.content:
The scream had come from the east wing, from the direction of Celia Pemberton's room. I found her braced against her doorframe, one hand clutching her wrapper at the throat, the other pressed flat against her chest as if she meant to hold her heart in place.

"A rat," she said. "It ran across my foot. I saw it—a shadow, then it was on me."

Her feet were bare. Her room was dark, the fire burned low. Calder arrived behind me, out of breath, and Elias came up the corridor with a lantern at his shoulder. We searched the room, the corridor, the wainscoting. No rat. No droppings. No trace of anything alive.

"There are no rats on the east wing, sir," Elias said quietly. "The cold keeps them below stairs."

Celia's gaze slid past me, down the corridor, to the splintered door of Arthur's suite—the door I had left open, the priest-hole gaping behind it. "It went into the wall," she added, with the vague certainty of a child. "The wainscoting."

A rat running into a wall. In a house where Arthur had written, in his own hand, that people lived in the walls. I let her keep her story. She was lying, or editing the truth, and I could not say which. Ruth Keene appeared at the far end of the corridor, still holding her leather purse, watching us with a stillness that was its own accusation. Then she was gone.

I did not return to the suite. Not yet. I went to Elias.

I found him in the doorway of the parlor, pale and narrow, watching me from the corner of his eye the way he watched everything. I made him give his account again, alone, in the dark dining room, with only his lantern between us.

"Tell me exactly what you saw outside Mr. Pemberton's door."

He spoke as if he were reading from a script. "There was a band of light under the door, sir. The lamp was burning inside. I saw a shadow pass over it."

"From which side?"

"From the fireplace side of the room. Moving toward the door. It stopped under the light for a moment." He swallowed. "Then Mr. Pemberton said, 'You're dead.'"

"Did he sound afraid?"

"No, sir. Astonished. As if he had seen something that should not exist."

That word had stuck in my mind since the first telling. Astonished. Not shouting, not terrified—astonished. He had looked at something and recognized it. Something that should not exist. A brother who was supposed to be dead.

I sent him away and stood alone in the dark, working it out.

The room had been sealed when we broke in. Door bolted from inside. Windows painted shut, the dust unbroken on the rails. Chimney too narrow for a child. The lamp had been burning. For a shadow to cross the band of light beneath the door, someone had to pass between the lamp and the door—someone inside the room. If Arthur had been alone, he could have made the shadow himself, moving across his own room. But he had not been alone. He had spoken to someone in astonishment. You do not say "You're dead" to your own shadow.

Therefore a second person had been inside that room while the bolt was already thrown. The killer had been there before Arthur locked himself in. And the only place in that room where a man could hide was the priest-hole.

Eight years of regret had taught me what happened when I built the outcome first and the evidence second. So I checked the reasoning again, slowly. It held. It held because it was built from what Elias had seen, not from what I hoped to prove.

The weapon had vanished with him. Two deep wounds, a defensive gash, and no blade anywhere in the room. If a second man had been inside, he had carried it out with him—through a door that was bolted, past windows that had not been opened in fifty years. There was only one place he could have gone to ground, and I had stood in it and called it empty.

Hours earlier, I had stood in that hole and found a fresh footprint, a cufflink, and the smell of stale tobacco. And I had found the brick back wall too regular—ruled like lines on a page. Mortar wanders over a century; this wall ran true. A wall built not to enclose a space but to make a space look sealed. I had been reaching for my penknife to press those bricks when Celia screamed.

A rat. On her foot. At midnight, in a wing where Elias swore there were no rats, at the exact moment I stood at the mouth of the secret.

No. Not a rat. Someone had wanted me away from that wall.

I went back up the stairs two at a time. The portrait of the two boys watched me pass—two identical smiles, the left one a dare—and I thought of Elias, who never looked at anything but that painting. The splintered door of Arthur's suite hung where Calder and I had forced it.

The panel in the wainscoting was still open. The lamp was where I had left it. The priest-hole breathed its cold air up at me, and with it the faint smell of stale tobacco.

I drew my penknife and started toward it. Somewhere in that black mouth was the door Arthur had drawn for me—a square with a line through it, a door without a frame. Not a door at all. A wall pretending to be one.

I would find what it was hiding. Even if I had to pull the wall down brick by brick.

chapters.name: The Forged Signature
chapters.content:
The bricks were too regular. I set the penknife to the seam and pressed.

The blade bit into the mortar line, and held. I was about to carve the truth out of that wall when I heard it—paper, crackling. Beneath it, the hungry whisper of flame. From Arthur's study, two doors down.

I pocketed the knife and moved.

The study door stood ajar. Through the gap, Ruth Keene knelt at the fireplace, feeding pages to a fire that had not caught. She did not hear me—her whole world was the burn.

I crossed the room, caught her wrist, and pulled the paper free. Heat came off it like a breath. Ruth fell back on her heels, and for one instant her face showed something raw. Grief, not guilt. Then the mask closed.

"Mr. Hale—"

"Get up."

I spread the smoking document flat under the lamp. The edges were charred, the corner eaten, but the words held. Power of Attorney. All of Arthur Pemberton's assets, transferred to Ruth Keene, effective upon his death. Dated the day before the murder.

And the signature: Arthur Pemberton.

It convinced for one glance. Then it collapsed. Arthur's real hand—the hand behind the letter folded in my pocket—was driven, impatient, slashing across the page. This hand had been careful. The pen lifted between strokes. The capital A had been traced twice, the second pass a hair's width off.

"Did you think the fire would destroy the ink?" I said.

She stood very straight. "I forged it. Yes." The words were flat, rehearsed. "But I wasn't stealing from Arthur. I was protecting him. From Marcus Webb."

"From Marcus."

"Marcus has been gutting the company for years. Arthur was too exhausted to see it, or too afraid to face it. I watched him do it, month after month. I told Arthur. He said he'd handle it. He never did. So I prepared this—so if Marcus moved, I could move first."

"Or use it. It transfers everything."

"I never used it." There was force behind it. "Arthur was alive until last night. I forged it to protect him from Marcus, not from Arthur."

I studied her for a long moment. "Is that all?"

"There's more." She looked at the door, then back at me. "I saw Marcus Webb enter Arthur's room earlier that night. A little after ten. I was watching the corridor—I wanted to catch him with his hands in the files, catch him for once—and I saw him go in through the door. He was inside for ten minutes. Then he came out and went back to the lounge. And then—" She stopped. "You know what happened after that."

I did. The scream. The bolted door. The body on the floor.

The door had been bolted from inside. If Marcus went through the door, Arthur had let him in—or Marcus had thrown the bolt himself before leaving. But the bolt had been thrown when Calder broke in. And no weapon sat in that room. No exit.

I found Webb in the lounge with a glass of whiskey three fingers deep. A low fire was the only light. When I told him what Ruth had said, he went the color of the embers and rose, spilling his drink as he did. "That woman is a liar. I never went near Arthur's room."

"She watched you."

"She saw what she wanted to see."

His words came too fast. I thought of the cufflink in my pocket, of the shadow Elias had seen cross the band of light, of a dead man's letter that said the answer was in the wall. A man who shouts his innocence in a quiet room may be shouting at his own reflection.

Celia Pemberton appeared in the doorway, silk robe, wine glass, watching us with the idle delight of a woman at a play. "Ask her about Paris," she said softly.

I looked at her.

"Paris," Celia repeated. "Three years ago. The business conference. Ask Ruth Keene how many beds Marcus Webb used that week."

The room went very quiet.

"They were lovers," Celia said. The word seemed to please her. "Not now, mind you. Past tense, I imagine. But it's a funny thing, isn't it? A woman who tells you her old flame entered a dead man's room—her word hangs on a history she forgot to mention."

Marcus was staring at the fire. Ruth stood in the study doorway, white as ash.

I looked at her. Properly, this time. And that was when I saw it: a dark smear on her sleeve. Oily black, catching the lamplight. The same grease that had marked the priest-hole floor where a man had stood waiting.

She saw me see it. Her face closed like a door. She turned and went down the corridor, and I did not stop her.

The priest-hole. She had sworn, on the truth of her face, that she had never known it existed. But the grease on her sleeve had come from its floor. Not from any office in this hotel—thick and cold, the kind a body leaves against old brick when it presses itself into hiding. I knew it because I had felt it under my own hand when I crawled out of that compartment. She had been inside the wall.

And the wall led somewhere.

I ran. Down the corridor, through the splintered door, into Arthur's suite. The panel still stood open, the priest-hole breathing cold air at me—black, waiting, full of the answers I had almost found.

I went in. The penknife was in my hand again.

chapters.name: The Boiler Room
chapters.content:
The bricks at the back of the priest-hole were too regular to be true, and a wall that works that hard at being a wall is lying.

I knelt with the lamp and the penknife and used the Armitage lesson the way it was meant to be used: I looked before I decided. I ran the blade along every mortar line. At the fourth course, near the right edge, the point sank into a seam that was not mortar at all—a line cut with a tool and hidden by coal dust. I traced it up, across, down. A clean rectangle the size of a door. Arthur's drawing. A door without a frame.

I pressed the knife into the seam and worked it. Under the heel of my palm the wall gave, a little, like a drawer that wanted to open. I pushed harder, and somewhere inside the brick a spring let go with a click I felt through the steel.

The back of the compartment swung toward me.

Beyond it, a passage opened, narrow and old, walled in lath and plaster, falling away to the left in a stair that vanished into black. The air changed on the third step—the glacier-cold of the niche became a smell of coal dust, rust, and old rot. I went down. The stairs doubled back, followed the bones of the house into its belly, and ended before an iron door furred with rust.

I set the lamp on the step, took the latch in both hands, and heaved. It gave with a groan that was the whole mountain turning over.

The boiler room opened like a cave.

Heat hit me first, then the smell of coal, oil, and hot metal. The boiler was a black iron cathedral with riveted seams, sighing to itself, its grate a banked orange glow. Pipes ran overhead like iron trees, dripping. The floor was concrete, gritty under my boots. I moved past the coal bin, and where the pipes bent away from the wall they left an alcove cut into the stone—the kind of pocket the men who built this house liked to hide.

The lamp found a coat first. Heavy wool, dark, and wet. Not damp—wet, still dripping at the cuffs. Somebody had been out in the storm and had come back in a hurry.

Beside it, a bundle in oilcloth. I unwrapped it. A kitchen knife, eight inches, honed to a wire edge. It had been wiped clean, but I knew what to look for. In the seam where the blade met the handle, the steel was dark, and I had looked at enough evidence to recognize what dried and was never quite cleaned.

Beneath the coat, a photograph.

Two boys in sailor suits, arm in arm. The portrait in the lounge, but older—faded, creased down the middle, corners soft as wool from years in a man's pocket. The left boy's smile was a dare.

I picked up the knife and stood.

The boiler sighed over my head. The lamp flame steadied. And then, riding against the furnace's breath, I heard a sound that did not belong: a slow exhalation, held back and then released, as if its owner had finally stopped pretending he was alone.

"Somebody's been living in these walls," I said, because the dark makes you speak to hear a voice.

"That he has."

The voice came from behind me.

I turned. The lamp threw the shadows back, and a man stood in the gap between the coal bin and the wall, where the dark ran deepest. He had been still so long he looked like part of the room.

He was gaunt. Not thin—starved down to the bone, a gray beard hiding the planes of his face, hair long and wild. His clothes had been good once, years ago, and had been lived in well past that.

But the face beneath the beard was Arthur Pemberton's face. The same eyes. The same jaw. The same mouth.

"Silas," I said.

"Victor Hale." He said my name as if he had known it a long time. "Arthur wrote to you for two years. He said you were the only one who would come." His voice was low and worn, and there was no anger in it. That frightened me more than shouting.

"You've been living down here."

"Days," he said. "I know these walls better than any living man. Arthur and I hid in them when we were boys. We played at being ghosts. Grown-ups walked past a foot away and never knew we were there." He nodded at the alcove. "The coat, the knife, the photograph. That's all I own. The things I came back for."

"You came back to kill him."

"I came back for my life." Still no heat. "Twenty years on that lake, Hale. He let the water take me and took the money. I survived it. I drank it. I breathed it. And I came home to collect what he owed me."

He was closer. I had not seen him move.

My hand was already inside my coat, closing on the revolver I had carried up the mountain without ever believing I would draw it. My fingers found the grip.

He was faster.

A length of black iron pipe came around in a flat arc, and by the time I understood what it was, it was too late. It caught me high on the side of the head and the world went sideways.

The lamp flew from my hand and died. My knees hit concrete. I folded over onto the floor, no pain yet, only a white noise swallowing my thoughts.

Behind my eyes the photograph burned: two boys in sailor suits, identical, the left one's smile a dare. And the truth came up out of the dark and closed over me like water.

There had never been a locked room.

Arthur had thrown the bolt because he believed he was alone. But the room held a man who had come in through the wall before the bolt ever fell. A man who waited in the priest-hole, stepped out, put two wounds in his brother's chest, and stepped back into the wall while the door stayed bolted and the world argued suicide.

The answer was in the wall.

Silas Pemberton was real.

I had found him.

The concrete was cold against my cheek. The boiler sighed. And the truth was still burning when the dark came down like the lid of a box.

chapters.name: The Twin
chapters.content:
The dark came back with heat and iron. My head rang like a bell struck once. My wrists were bound behind me, rope biting to the bone, lashed to the pipe that fed the boiler. The furnace grate glowed orange, and the room smelled of coal and hot metal.

Silas Pemberton stood with his back to me, feeding the knife into the fire.

The blade turned from gray to red. I was alive, which meant he wanted something, and so I stayed quiet and watched him. When he turned, Arthur Pemberton's face looked at me out of a stranger's beard.

"You know why I came?"

"Arthur wrote to me for two years," I said. "He thought you were a ghost. Then he stopped thinking that."

Silas crouched. "Twenty years ago we went out on that lake in a boat that was never seaworthy. The water took us both. One plank held one brother. I reached for it, and I saw Arthur's face when he made the choice. He left me to the water and took everything that should have been half mine." He said it flat, like scripture. "A fishing boat dragged me out at dawn. I've been waiting ever since."

"Through the priest-hole," I said. "You were already in the room before he threw the bolt."

His eyes caught the furnace light. "You found the wall."

"The brick was too regular. The seam was too clean."

"I knew these walls better than he did because I never stopped living in them. I was in the suite when Arthur came in. I heard the brass slide home. I waited until he'd settled by the fire, thinking he was safe, and then I stepped out of the wall." He paused. "He said, 'You're dead.' Astonished. Like he'd seen God wearing his own face."

"The shadow Elias saw under the door. That was you, crossing the room."

"I wanted him to see me coming." He glanced at the furnace, where the blade now glowed white. "Two wounds in the chest. One on the arm he tried to fight me off with. Then I stepped back into the wall. The bolt stayed thrown. The room stayed locked. The world argued suicide while I walked home." He smiled. "There was never a locked room, Hale. Only a room a man believed was closed."

I tested the rope. It didn't give. My gun was somewhere in the dark, and I was bound to an iron pipe with a man who'd waited twenty years to finish the thing he'd started.

So I talked.

"Arthur feared you," I said. "That's the thing that broke him. His last letter wasn't a letter. It was a confession." I held his eyes. "He said, 'I let him drown. I wanted the money, and I let the water take him.' He carried you his whole life, Silas. Not guilt. Fear. He saw you on the funicular. Outside his window. He was never the brother who won. He was the brother afraid of losing."

Silas went still.

"What did you come back to collect?" I asked. "Money? The name? Or did you just want him to see the brother he'd left in the water, standing in front of him, telling him he was dead?"

For a moment, the only sound was the boiler's deep sigh. Then he said, quiet: "I came back for my life. The one he owed me."

"Then you've got it. You're standing in the light. He's dead in a room only you could open. You don't need to burn anything else."

"You think I'm done?"

"I think you're still here talking to a man you could have killed already. Which means the telling matters." I let that sit. "I've got all night, Silas. So do you."

Behind him, the iron door at the top of the stair clicked.

Silas didn't hear it. I did.

The door crashed open. "Sheriff! Freeze!" Calder came down the stairs with his lamp swinging and his revolver up, Elias at his heels like a pale knife. Silas lunged for the iron pipe at his feet, but Calder fired once, high, and the bullet rang off the boiler in a shower of sparks. It was enough. Elias drove into him, wiry and hard, and they went down on the concrete together.

It took three of us to hold him. Calder had the cuffs on before his lamp stopped swaying.

He looked at me tied to the pipe, at the white-hot knife in the furnace, at the gaunt man wearing his brother's face. He crouched and worked at the rope on my wrists.

"Found your note under the door," he said. "Took Elias showing me the panel to move me." He pulled the rope free. "You said follow the wall."

"The wall opened."

Calder looked at Silas, then at the room, then back at me. He was my old rival, and I'd been waiting half my life for this. He gave it to me flat and honest.

"I was wrong," he said. "There was never a locked room. The killer was already inside." He pulled me to my feet. "Good work, Hale."

I stood in the furnace light, and for the first time in six years, my hands didn't shake at the sound of my own name.

chapters.name: Redemption
chapters.content:
Calder let me sit in Arthur's room as the blizzard broke. The first light came over the glacier, white and hard, filling the window like water filling a glass. For three days the wind had buried us alive; now it was gone, and the peaks stood out clean as cut bone. The world that had held us closed had opened again.

The funicular crew reached the top by mid-morning, and the deputies went through the hidden passage with lamps, measuring it from priest-hole to boiler room. Elias showed them where the old service door gave onto the glacier path. Silas had come and gone through the storm that way. No phantom. No legend. Just a man who knew the walls. Elias never explained how he knew the walls himself. I didn't ask. I owed him too much to make him lie to me.

They took Silas down in the noon car. I watched from the lounge window as he stepped off into the white basin, handcuffed, gaunt, wearing Arthur's face. He did not look back. The photograph of two boys in sailor suits went down with him in an evidence envelope, and the knife went too—white-hot from the furnace, warped, its blade ruined for any courtroom. But he had confessed, to me and to Calder, and that would have to be enough. Whatever other debt he'd come to collect, the courts would set its price.

The cufflink I'd found in the priest-hole went into a second envelope with a note in my hand. Silas never asked about it. Some things a man leaves behind and doesn't care to claim.

Celia left that morning, her scream never fully explained. Ruth and Webb followed at noon, strangers bound by nothing but a funeral. I did not ask what was in Ruth's purse. I had secrets of my own, and I was done carrying them.

I went back to Arthur's room one last time when the hotel was quiet. The bolt lay where Calder had dropped it. The wainscoting stood open, the priest-hole exposed for the cramped, ordinary space it was—a hollow in the wall, nothing more. No trick. No miracle. A man had stepped out of it, killed his brother, and stepped back inside while the bolt stayed thrown. There had never been a locked room. Only a room I had insisted was locked.

That was the wound I carried, the one that had cost me my badge. I had built my whole identity on certainty. The Armitage case taught me that certainty could lie, and instead of learning the lesson, I had learned to tighten my grip. I searched that room for exits I had already decided could not exist, because the alternative—that my judgment might be wrong—was a door I refused to open. Arthur had sent me a map, and I measured the frame while the door stood waiting. The key was never a key at all. It was a man who had already been inside—and the door I truly had to open was the one to my own closed mind.

I sat at his desk and wrote the first letter. To Arthur. I told him I believed him—too late, but I believed. That he'd been right about the walls and right about me. That I was sorry I'd made him dead before I finally listened.

Then I wrote the second. To the court. The Armitage case. The evidence I'd ignored, the other man's guilt, my perfect certainty. I wrote his name and mine and the word I'd never been able to say. I signed both letters before I could stop myself.

Calder found me at the desk. He read the second letter over my shoulder and let out a long breath.

"You were right about the room," he said at last. "About everything. You're reopening Armitage."

"I should have done it six years ago."

He looked at my hands, folded over the letter. Steady.

"Good," he said, and left me to finish.

The funicular came back up the mountain in the empty afternoon. I stood at the top of the tracks in the cold bright air, the apology to Arthur folded in my coat, the truth on its way to the judges who had once believed me. I knew better now. The key to a locked room is never a key. It is the willingness to say four words and mean them: I could be wrong. The moment I said them, the door in my own mind swung open—and I rode the daylight down the mountain a free man.
